title: Errors and Debugging
summary: Debugging means finding and fixing mistakes in a program. Error messages give clues about what went wrong.
introduction: Debugging means finding and fixing mistakes in a program. Error messages give clues about what went wrong. Work like a detective. Read the message, check one line at a time and use console messages to see your values.
learningObjectives: Identify the common error types from their names and messages
Recover from failures with try, catch and finally
Throw descriptive errors, including custom classes and a cause
Debug with console methods, breakpoints and the debugger statement

blocks.text: When something goes wrong at runtime, JavaScript creates an **error object** and stops the current function. Unhandled, it stops the whole script and the console shows three things: the error **name** (its type), the **message** (what went wrong) and the **stack trace** (which function called which, with file names and line numbers). Read the first line, then the first stack frame that points at your own file; that is almost always where the bug is.

rows: A typo in the code itself; nothing runs until it is fixed
Using a variable that was never declared, or before its `let`/`const` line
A value is not what you assumed: `null` instead of an element, a string instead of a function
A number outside the allowed range, or a function calling itself forever

blocks.text: The helper below runs a few deliberately broken snippets and prints the name and message of each error. The wording is Chrome's; Firefox and Safari phrase the same errors slightly differently, which is why code should check `error.name` or `instanceof`, never the message text.

blocks.text: `try` wraps code that might fail. If an error is thrown anywhere inside it, execution jumps straight to `catch`, which receives the error object, and the rest of the `try` block is skipped. `finally` runs afterwards in every case, even when `try` or `catch` ends with `return`, which makes it the right place for cleanup such as hiding a loading spinner. Catch only what you can handle: a parsing failure you can report to the user, yes; a typo in your own code, no, because that needs fixing, not hiding.

Checked "abc"

blocks.title: The empty catch block
blocks.text: `try { ... } catch {}` with nothing inside makes failures invisible: the script carries on with missing data and the real bug surfaces somewhere else, much later. At minimum log the error; better, show the user a message or rethrow it. If you really intend to ignore a specific failure, write a comment saying why.

blocks.content:
undefined
Using defaults because: SyntaxError
light

blocks.text: `throw` raises an error from your own code when input or state is invalid. Throw `Error` objects (or subclasses), never plain strings, so the stack trace and `name` are available. A **custom error class** lets callers distinguish your errors with `instanceof`, and the `cause` option attaches the original low-level error to a higher-level one so neither explanation is lost. The class syntax is explained in the [Modules and Classes](/tutorials/javascript/modules-classes) lesson.

blocks.content:
true
ValidationError on email: Email must contain @
Could not load settings
SyntaxError

blocks.text: The quickest debugging tool is a temporary `console.log` that prints a value where you suspect the problem; `console.warn` and `console.error` print the same way with a colour and a stack trace, and `console.table(array)` shows an array of objects as a grid in the developer tools. For anything beyond a quick look, use a **breakpoint**: open the Sources tab (Debugger in Firefox), click a line number, and the browser pauses there so you can inspect every variable and step through the code line by line. Writing `debugger;` in your code sets the same breakpoint from the inside.

debug: pen -> 3
debug: book -> 12
total = 15
Cart has fewer than 3 items
This is what an error log looks like

items: Read the whole error: name, message, and the first stack frame in your own file.
Reproduce it reliably. A bug you can trigger on demand is half fixed.
Form a hypothesis (*the element is null because the script runs too early*) and test it with one log or breakpoint.
Fix the cause, not the symptom: a `?.` that hides a `null` is rarely the real fix.
Remove the temporary logs, then keep a regression check, for example a unit test with [Jest](/tutorials/jest) or [Vitest](/tutorials/vitest).

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Take the `parseAge` function and add a third rule: the input must not be empty. Decide which error type fits, throw it with a helpful message, and confirm that `finally` still runs for the new case.

questions.question: Which error does `console.log(undeclaredName + 1)` throw?
questions.explanation: Reading a name that was never declared throws a ReferenceError. A TypeError would appear if the value existed but was used in an impossible way.

questions.question: A missing closing bracket in your script file can be caught with try...catch inside the same file.
questions.explanation: A SyntaxError in the file itself happens while parsing, before any code runs, so no try block has a chance to catch it. Only runtime errors (including a SyntaxError thrown by JSON.parse) can be caught.
